title: A feasibility study comparing vacuum drainage with a surgical cut to treat breast abscesses
official: A randomised controlled trial of radiological vacuum drainage compared with surgical incision drainage for large, multiloculated or needle aspiration-resistant breast abscesses, assessing patient satisfaction at 3 months following intervention
summary:
Background and study aims
A breast abscess is a painful collection of infected fluid or pus in the breast. It can occur during breastfeeding and may need to be drained to help the infection settle. One way to do this is through surgery, where a cut is made in the breast to drain the pus. However, surgery can leave a visible scar and may affect the shape of the breast.
This study is looking at another treatment called vacuum-assisted drainage. This uses a small tube and gentle suction to remove the infected fluid. The researchers want to find out whether it is practical and acceptable to compare vacuum-assisted drainage with surgery in a randomised study. They will also look at quality of life, pain, how quickly symptoms improve, whether further treatment is needed, and women's experiences of treatment. The findings will help the researchers plan a larger study in the future.

Who can participate?
Women aged 18 years or older with a breast abscess confirmed by an ultrasound scan may be able to take part. The abscess must be larger than 5 cm, have more than one pocket of infected fluid, or have already been unsuccessfully treated with needle drainage.
Women cannot take part if, for example, they have breast cancer, certain other types of breast inflammation or abscess, skin damage that requires surgery, or a condition or treatment that increases their risk of bleeding.

What does the study involve? (for participants)
The study aims to recruit 70 women from 26 hospitals. Participants are randomly allocated to receive either vacuum-assisted drainage or surgical drainage.
Vacuum-assisted drainage is usually carried out under local anaesthetic in an outpatient setting. A small cut of about 5 to 6 mm is made in the skin. A vacuum drainage device is then guided into the abscess using an ultrasound scan, and gentle suction is used to remove the infected fluid. Participants can usually return home soon afterwards if there are no immediate problems.
Surgical drainage usually requires admission to hospital and is normally carried out under general anaesthetic. A cut is made in the breast to drain the abscess. The area is cleaned and a drain is usually left in place for several days. Participants return home when they are well enough.
Participants in both groups are followed up to check their recovery and wound healing and to make sure that the abscess has not returned. Quality of life is assessed before treatment and 3 months afterwards. Pain during the procedure, how long symptoms take to improve, further treatment, breastfeeding and healthcare costs are also assessed. Some patients and clinicians will be invited to take part in interviews about their experiences of the treatment and study.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Both treatments are designed to drain the breast abscess and help the infection settle. Vacuum-assisted drainage may avoid a larger surgical cut and a general anaesthetic. However, it is not yet known whether vacuum-assisted drainage is better than surgery, which is why this study is being carried out.
Possible problems include pain, bleeding, problems with wound healing, the abscess returning, or the treatment not fully draining the abscess. Some participants may need further treatment. Surgery may also result in scarring or changes to the shape of the breast.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being carried out in England. Participating centres listed in the study record include Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust at St Mary's Hospital in London and Gateshead Health NHS Foundation Trust at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Gateshead (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to June 2028.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Professor Daniel Leff, d.leff@imperial.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Female
2. 18 years or older
3. Confirmed breast abscess on ultrasound scan imaging
4. Breast abscess size >5cm, and/or multiloculated, and/or that has one failed attempt at 19G needle aspiration
Exclusion criteria:
1. Concurrent breast cancer diagnosis
2. Cancerous mastitis
3. Biopsy confirmed granulomatous infection
4. Periductal non-lactational abscess
5. Skin necrosis requiring surgical debridement
6. Anticoagulation or bleeding dyscrasias
